pages.c08-p02: Describe the advantages of cloud computing for an organisation
pages.c08-p03: Describe the disadvantages of cloud computing for an organisation
pages.c08-p04: Describe the impact of cloud computing on gaming
pages.c08-p05: Describe the impact of cloud computing on file storage and file sharing, including collaborative tools

q.q: Which is the best definition of cloud computing?
o: Storing files on a server in the organisation's own building, reached over its LAN
Using software that has been installed on the hard drive of your own computer
Connecting a laptop, tablet or phone to the internet using a Wi-Fi network
Using storage and software on remote servers, accessed on demand over the internet
q.why: Cloud computing needs both ideas: resources held on remote servers and accessed on demand over the internet. An organisation's own server is local computing.

q.q: Where is data that is saved 'in the cloud' physically stored?
o: On servers in a cloud provider's data centre
Nowhere physical, because cloud data is virtual
In the memory of the user's home router
On the hard drive of the device that saved it
q.why: The cloud is not magic storage in the sky; it is real computers in data centres owned by a provider.

q.q: What is a data centre?
o: A room in a school where pupils' laptops are charged and stored overnight
A piece of software that synchronises files between a phone and a laptop
A building full of servers run by a provider such as Microsoft, Google or Amazon
A single hard drive that stores every file uploaded to the internet
q.why: Cloud providers run their remote servers in huge data centres.

q.q: Which of these is an example of cloud storage?
o: An internal SSD
A USB memory stick
A school's local file server
Google Drive
q.why: Google Drive saves files on a provider's remote servers. The others are local storage.

q.q: Which of these is an example of cloud software?
o: A word processor installed from a disc
Google Docs used in a web browser
A game stored on a console's hard drive
An app saved on a memory card
q.why: Cloud software runs in a browser or app from remote servers, for example Microsoft 365 online, Google Docs or Canva.

q.q: Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services are examples of which type of cloud service?
o: Cloud gaming services that stream games to players' screens
Cloud platforms that rent servers and processing power to businesses
Cloud storage services that save pupils' homework files
Cloud software used to write documents in a browser
q.why: Azure and AWS are cloud platforms for businesses, giving rented servers and processing power.

q.q: Xbox Cloud Gaming and GeForce NOW are examples of which type of cloud service?
o: Cloud storage
Cloud platforms for businesses
Cloud gaming
Cloud software for documents
q.why: In cloud gaming, games run on remote servers and are streamed to the player.

q.q: How do organisations normally pay for cloud computing?
o: A single payment when the provider builds its data centre
Nothing, because cloud services are always free of charge
A fee for each device that is connected to the internet
A subscription, or pay as you go for what they actually use
q.why: Organisations normally pay a subscription or pay as you go for what they use.

q.q: What does 'pay as you go' mean for a cloud service?
o: The organisation pays only for the resources it actually uses
The organisation pays one fixed fee no matter how much it uses
The organisation pays before it can see what is on offer
The organisation pays for the servers and then owns them
q.why: Pay as you go means paying only for what is used, rather than a fixed amount.

q.q: A pupil saves homework to OneDrive at school. Why can she open it at home on her phone?
o: The file was copied onto her phone's memory when she saved it at school
The school's network automatically emails a copy of every file to pupils
OneDrive files are stored in the phone's SIM card so they go everywhere
The file is on remote servers that any internet-connected device can reach
q.why: Cloud data is held on a provider's remote servers, so it can be reached from any device with an internet connection.

q.q: With cloud computing, who maintains the servers that store the data?
o: The user of each device
The cloud provider
The organisation's own technician
The user's broadband router
q.why: With local computing the user or organisation maintains the equipment; with cloud computing the provider does.

q.q: With local computing, where is data stored?
o: On the device's own drive or the organisation's own server
On a provider's remote servers in a data centre
On servers rented from a cloud platform such as Azure
On a storage service such as iCloud or Dropbox
q.why: Local computing stores data on the device itself or on the organisation's own server; cloud computing uses a provider's remote servers.

q.q: With local computing, how can the data normally be reached?
o: From any device with an internet connection
Only through a web browser on a phone
Only from that device or the organisation's network
From any device that has cloud gaming
q.why: Local data can only be reached from that device or network; cloud data can be reached from any internet-connected device.

q.q: A pupil defines cloud computing as 'storing stuff online'. Why would this not earn two marks?
o: It should have said that the cloud is a single place in the sky
It does not mention remote servers or on-demand access over the internet clearly
It should have named a USB stick as an example of the cloud
It is wrong, because cloud computing never involves storage
q.why: A two-mark definition needs two ideas: data or software held on remote servers, and accessed over the internet on demand. 'Storing stuff online' is too vague.

q.q: Why do internet access and trust in the provider both matter for cloud computing?
o: The cloud is a single shared hard drive that every internet user can open
The data is on real computers owned by a provider and reached over the internet
The provider needs the user's password to switch on the user's own device
Cloud data is only copied to the user's device once a month by the provider
q.why: The cloud is real computers in data centres owned by a provider, which is why internet access and trust in that provider both matter.

q.q: Which statement about cloud computing is correct?
o: Data can only be reached from the computer that first saved it
Programs must be installed on each device before they can be used
Data and programs can be reached from a PC, laptop, tablet or phone
Data is stored inside the router at the user's home
q.why: Any device with an internet connection can reach cloud data and programs.

q.q: Which word in the definition of cloud computing means the resources are available whenever they are needed?
o: Remote
On demand
Local
Scalable
q.why: Cloud resources are delivered on demand over the internet. 'Remote' describes where the servers are.

q.q: Which service is the odd one out because it is NOT a cloud service?
o: Microsoft 365 used online in a browser
Software installed only on a laptop's own hard drive
Files saved to iCloud from an iPhone
Games streamed through GeForce NOW
q.why: Software installed on the laptop's own drive is local computing. The other three are delivered from remote servers over the internet.

q.q: Why is cloud computing often cost effective for an organisation?
o: It does not need to buy and maintain its own servers
Cloud subscriptions never rise in price over time
It no longer needs any internet connection at all
The provider pays the organisation for its data
q.why: The organisation avoids buying and maintaining servers and many software licences, and with pay as you go pays only for what it uses.

q.q: What does it mean to say that cloud computing is scalable?
o: Files are compressed so they take up less space on servers
The service is free for small organisations and charities
The same software runs on any make of computer or phone
Resources can be increased or reduced quickly as needs change
q.why: Scalability means storage, users and bandwidth can be increased or reduced quickly to match demand.

q.q: A garden centre is very busy every spring. Why does scalability suit it?
o: It can buy more servers that will be busy for the whole year
It can stop paying for the cloud during the busy spring months
It can move all its files back onto USB sticks in the summer
It can pay for extra capacity for a few months, then drop back
q.why: A seasonal business can pay for extra capacity when busy and drop back afterwards, instead of buying servers that sit idle most of the year.

q.q: A design studio runs out of cloud storage. What is the advantage of the cloud in this situation?
o: Old files are deleted automatically to free up space for new ones
More space can be bought instantly without installing any hardware
The studio must buy a larger server and install it in the office
The provider moves the files onto staff members' own laptops
q.why: Cloud storage offers large capacity, and more can be bought instantly without installing hardware.

q.q: Which advantage of the cloud removes the need for staff to install security patches themselves?
o: Pay as you go pricing for storage
Real-time collaboration on files
Large storage capacity
Automatic software updates by the provider
q.why: The provider applies updates and security patches, saving staff time.

q.q: How does cloud computing help with backup and recovery?
o: Each member of staff must copy files to a USB stick each night
The provider backs up data automatically and can restore it
Files are only stored on the device that created them
Files are deleted when the subscription is renewed
q.why: The provider backs up data automatically and can restore it, so no separate backup devices or procedures are needed.

q.q: A council office floods overnight, but staff can still reach all their files the next day from home. Why?
o: The flood water cannot damage modern office servers
The data is held off site in the provider's data centre
The files were stored on the office's own local server
The cloud provider pays to repair the office equipment
q.why: Cloud storage protects against local disasters: if the office floods, the data is still safe in the provider's data centre.

q.q: How does the cloud support home and hybrid working?
o: Staff can reach files anywhere, any time, on any internet-connected device
Staff can only open files when they are inside the office building
Staff no longer need any internet connection when working from home
Staff must take the office server home with them each evening
q.why: Accessibility from any internet-connected device supports home and hybrid working.

q.q: Which cloud advantage lets several staff work on the same file at the same time?
o: Scalability
Automatic updates
Collaboration
Pay as you go
q.why: Collaboration means several people can work on the same file at once.

q.q: Why can moving to the cloud reduce the carbon footprint of an organisation's own premises?
o: Data centres use no electricity at all because they are run on solar power
Cloud files are smaller than local files, so they use less electricity
Staff must switch off their computers whenever they use cloud software
Less equipment in the building means less electricity for servers and cooling
q.why: The carbon footprint point is about the organisation's own premises: fewer servers means less electricity used for running and cooling them.

q.q: Which statement about the cloud and carbon footprint is accurate?
o: Moving to the cloud removes all of the electricity used by an organisation's IT
Data centres use less electricity than one office PC because they are virtual
Data centres still use a lot of electricity, though large providers often run them efficiently
Cloud computing always increases an organisation's carbon footprint on site
q.why: The saving is on the organisation's own site. Data centres still use a lot of electricity, though big providers often run them more efficiently than small server rooms.

q.q: A pupil writes 'The cloud is cheaper.' How could this be improved to earn the mark?
o: Add that the cloud is a type of computer that is stored in the sky
Add that the cloud is cheaper because it uses a faster connection
Add that the organisation does not have to buy and maintain its own servers
Nothing, because 'cheaper' on its own is a full answer
q.why: 'It is cheaper' earns nothing alone; examiners want the reason, such as saving on buying and maintaining servers and technician costs.

q.q: A start-up has five staff but expects to grow quickly. Which cloud advantage is most relevant to its growth?
o: Users and storage can be added quickly as the business grows
Data is protected if the office is burgled or flooded
The provider applies security patches automatically
Several staff can comment on the same file together
q.why: Scalability lets a growing business add users, storage and bandwidth quickly without buying new hardware.

q.q: Which of these is an advantage of cloud computing for an organisation?
o: Staff can work without any internet connection
Protection from local disasters such as fire or burglary
The organisation keeps full control over where data is stored
Subscription costs end after the first year
q.why: Off-site storage protects against local disasters. The other statements are untrue or describe the opposite of cloud drawbacks.

q.q: Why can cloud computing reduce an organisation's software licence costs?
o: Software used in the cloud is never protected by copyright law
It does not need to buy and manage many software licences of its own
Cloud software is always free for organisations of any size
Staff can share one licence key with anyone they like
q.why: Cost effectiveness includes not needing to buy and maintain its own servers or many software licences.

q.q: Which pair of cloud advantages would best help a district council whose staff now work from several towns?
o: Carbon footprint and large storage
Accessibility and collaboration
Automatic updates and pay as you go
Scalability and protection from disasters
q.why: Staff spread across several towns most need to reach files from anywhere and work on the same files together.

q.q: Why do examiners want 'why it matters' as well as the name of a cloud advantage?
o: A named advantage alone, such as 'cheaper', usually earns nothing without the reason
The name of the advantage is not needed if the explanation is long enough
Examiners only award marks for advantages that are written as a list
Only disadvantages need explaining; advantages can be a single word
q.why: Each advantage needs to be explained with why it helps the organisation; a bare word such as 'cheaper' earns nothing.

q.q: A two-person design studio wants to avoid paying a technician to look after servers. Which cloud feature helps most?
o: The provider maintains the servers and applies updates
Files can be shared with a link instead of an attachment
Version history shows who changed each design
Data can be reached from a tablet as well as a PC
q.why: With the cloud the provider maintains the servers and applies updates, saving hardware and technician costs.

q.q: Which advantage of the cloud means an organisation does not need separate backup devices or procedures?
o: Backup and recovery by the provider
Scalability of storage and users
Collaboration on shared files
Accessibility from any device
q.why: The provider backs up data automatically and can restore it.

q.q: Why might a business choose to buy cloud storage rather than more local hard drives?
o: Local hard drives cannot store photos or video files at all
Cloud storage never needs any kind of internet connection
Cloud storage offers far more space and can be expanded instantly
Local hard drives are only allowed to be used at home
q.why: Cloud storage gives far more space than local drives, and more can be bought instantly without installing hardware.

q.q: Which advantage is about the organisation not having to keep buying servers that sit idle most of the year?
o: Scalability
Collaboration
Accessibility
Automatic updates
q.why: Scalability lets capacity rise and fall with demand, so idle servers are not needed.

q.q: Which statement about cloud advantages is correct?
o: Cloud storage stops staff ever losing access to their files
Cloud computing means the organisation no longer has to pay for IT
Cloud providers cannot see or affect an organisation's data
Staff need no technical knowledge to have their data backed up by the provider
q.why: The provider handles backup and recovery. The cloud can still have downtime, costs money and depends on the provider.

q.q: Why is a reliable internet connection essential for an organisation using the cloud?
o: If the connection fails, staff cannot reach their files or software
The connection speed decides how much the subscription costs
Cloud software only works when the internet is not in use
The connection stores a backup copy of every file
q.why: All cloud access is over the internet, so if the broadband or router fails, work stops.

q.q: Which is the best explanation of a cloud disadvantage?
o: It needs an internet connection, so if the broadband fails staff cannot access files
It needs an internet connection, which is a disadvantage for the organisation
It needs the internet, so it is not good for some businesses that use it
It needs internet access and a router, and it costs money every month
q.why: Examiners want the consequence: 'so if the broadband fails staff cannot access their files'. A bare 'needs internet' scores one mark at most.

q.q: What is downtime?
o: A period when a service is unavailable
The time taken to download a file
Cheaper rates at off-peak times
The time taken to log off a system
q.why: Downtime means the service cannot be used, for example during a provider outage or a broadband fault.

q.q: A cloud provider has an outage. Why is this a particular problem for its customers?
o: Their data is deleted from the provider's servers permanently
Their subscription fees are refunded automatically
Their data is unavailable and they cannot fix the problem themselves
Their files are moved back to their own local servers
q.why: Provider outages or maintenance make data unavailable, and the organisation cannot fix it itself.

q.q: Many businesses that rely on the cloud keep a 4G router. Why?
o: To make the cloud provider's servers run faster
To avoid paying for a cloud subscription
To store a copy of their data on the router
As a backup connection if the main broadband fails
q.why: Downtime is the biggest practical worry, so many businesses keep a backup connection such as a 4G router.

q.q: Why can bandwidth limits be a disadvantage of a cloud plan?
o: Bandwidth limits stop more than one person logging on at once
The organisation may be charged extra if it exceeds its allowance
Bandwidth limits mean files can only be stored for a month
Bandwidth limits prevent files from being shared with links
q.why: Some plans include a limited allowance and charge extra if it is exceeded.

q.q: A video company has a slow internet line. Which cloud disadvantage will affect it most?
o: Its files will not be backed up by the provider
It will not be able to add any more storage
Its staff will not be able to share links
Uploading its large files will take a long time
q.why: Uploading large files over a slow line takes a long time.

q.q: Which is a security and privacy disadvantage of cloud computing?
o: Files are backed up automatically by the provider each day
Staff can open files from home on their own devices
Storage can be increased quickly when it is needed
Data is held by a third party and could be exposed in a data breach
q.why: Data held by a third party could be exposed in a breach. The other three are advantages.

q.q: A firm stores its customers' personal data with a cloud provider. Who is still responsible for that data under the UK GDPR?
o: Only the cloud provider
The customers themselves
The firm itself
Nobody, once it is in the cloud
q.why: An organisation storing personal data in the cloud is still responsible for it under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

q.q: Which body can investigate an organisation that fails to protect personal data it stores in the cloud?
o: The cloud provider's customer support team
The organisation's internet service provider
The Information Commission (formerly the ICO)
The manufacturer of the organisation's servers
q.why: The Information Commission (formerly the ICO) can investigate if personal data is not protected.

q.q: Which laws require an organisation to protect personal data it stores in the cloud?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the UK GDPR
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
The Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: The organisation is still responsible for personal data under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

q.q: Why are the ongoing costs of cloud computing a disadvantage?
o: The organisation must pay once for every server in the data centre
The organisation must buy new laptops each year to use the cloud
Subscriptions never end, may rise, and grow with storage and users
The cloud costs nothing at first but must be bought outright later
q.why: Subscriptions never end and may rise; costs grow as storage and users increase.

q.q: Why can customer support be a disadvantage of using the cloud?
o: The provider will not answer any questions about its service
Support is only available by visiting the data centre in person
Customers have to repair the provider's servers themselves
Help may be slow, or cost extra, when something goes wrong
q.why: Customer support may be slow or cost extra when there is a problem.

q.q: Why does cloud computing mean an organisation has less control?
o: It depends on the provider's decisions, prices and data centre locations
It cannot choose which members of staff can open which of its files
It has to let the provider decide which software its staff will learn
It must store its files on the computers of other organisations
q.why: The organisation depends on the provider's decisions, prices and where its data centres are, and moving provider can be hard.

q.q: Why can it be difficult for an organisation to leave its cloud provider?
o: Moving all its data and systems to another provider can be hard
Cloud providers are not allowed to give data back to customers
The law says each organisation must keep the same provider
Data stored in the cloud can never be downloaded again
q.why: Less control includes the fact that moving to another provider can be hard.

q.q: Most of the disadvantages of cloud computing follow from which fact?
o: Cloud software is always slower than software installed on a local computer
Cloud storage is much smaller than the storage on a local hard drive
Data and software are in someone else's hands, reached over someone else's network
Cloud providers only allow one member of staff to log in at a time
q.why: Cloud computing moves the organisation's data and software into someone else's hands, reached over someone else's network; most drawbacks follow from that.

q.q: A solicitor's office in Omagh is considering moving client files to the cloud. Which concern is most specific to the type of data it holds?
o: Its staff will be able to reach their files from home on a laptop or tablet
Confidential personal data is held by a third party and could be exposed in a breach
The provider will apply updates and security patches to its software
It will be able to buy more storage quickly as the business grows
q.why: A solicitor holds confidential personal data, so security and privacy of data held by a third party is the key concern. The other options are advantages.

q.q: Which of these is NOT a disadvantage of cloud computing for an organisation?
o: Work stops if the broadband fails
Data is protected if the office has a fire
Subscription costs may rise
The provider may suffer an outage
q.why: Protection from local disasters is an advantage. The other three are disadvantages.

q.q: Which statement compares cloud and local storage correctly when the internet connection fails?
o: Local files can still be opened, but cloud files cannot be reached
Cloud files can still be opened, but local files cannot be reached
Neither local files nor cloud files can be opened at all
Both can be opened, because the cloud stores files in the router
q.why: Local files are on the device or organisation's own server, so they still work; cloud files are reached over the internet, so a failed connection stops access.

q.q: Which is the most complete explanation of the risk of provider downtime?
o: During an outage at the provider, the organisation may have to pay a bit more for its subscription
During an outage at the provider, the organisation's data is moved to a different country for safety
During an outage at the provider, staff must drive to the data centre to collect copies of their files
During an outage at the provider, data is unavailable and the organisation can only wait for it to be fixed
q.why: The problem is that the data is unavailable and the organisation cannot fix the provider's problem itself.

q.q: How have cloud technologies reduced distribution costs for game producers?
o: Games are now stored on cheaper discs that cost less to post to shops
Producers pay data centres to give games away free to all players
Games are only sold in shops that are owned by the producer
Games are sold and downloaded online, so there are no discs to make or shops to pay
q.why: Selling and downloading games online means producers no longer pay to make discs or for shops to sell them; savings can mean lower prices.

q.q: Why are games that run or are checked online harder to pirate?
o: They are protected by a stronger type of plastic disc
They are much harder to copy illegally than discs
They can only be played in an official game shop
They are always given away free, so nobody copies them
q.why: Games run or checked online are much harder to copy illegally than discs, protecting sales and funding for new games.

q.q: A games studio in Belfast sells its new game online. Which impact of the cloud does this show?
o: Lower latency for players in other countries
Players needing a more powerful console
Access to a global market, increasing sales
Less need for the studio to release updates
q.why: Online sales give a studio a global market, increasing sales and profit.

q.q: How does the cloud help a game producer fix a bug found after release?
o: New discs must be posted to every player who bought it
Players must take their console back to the shop
The bug can only be fixed in the next version of the game
Patches are delivered through game servers immediately
q.why: Patches, fixes and extra content are delivered through game servers immediately.

q.q: Why do game producers offer free demos online?
o: Demos stop the full game being pirated
Demos reduce the latency of the full game
Demos let players skip buying the full game
Free trial versions attract new customers
q.why: Demos are free trial versions that attract new customers.

q.q: What does 'instant release' mean for players of downloadable games?
o: They can play the game before it has been made
They must wait for the game to reach the shops
They can download a game the moment it launches
They can only play the game once it is updated
q.why: Players download a game the moment it launches instead of waiting for it to reach shops.

q.q: In cloud gaming, where does the game actually run?
o: On the processor of the player's phone
On the player's home broadband router
On powerful servers in a data centre
On a disc inserted into a console
q.why: In cloud gaming the game runs on servers in a data centre and video is streamed back to the player.

q.q: In cloud gaming, what is sent between the player and the server?
o: The whole game is downloaded first and then the player's saves are uploaded
Video of the player is sent up and the controller settings are sent back
Controller inputs go up to the server and video of the game is streamed back
The player's console sends the game disc data to the server to be checked
q.why: The player's controller inputs are sent up and video of the game is streamed back.

q.q: Why can a player enjoy high-quality graphics on a cheap tablet using cloud gaming?
o: The tablet downloads extra graphics memory from the cloud
The game is processed on powerful remote servers, not on the tablet
Cloud games use simpler graphics than console games
The tablet's screen is upgraded by the cloud provider
q.why: Because the game runs on powerful servers, high-quality graphics can be played on cheap devices without buying the newest console.

q.q: What is latency?
o: The total amount of data a game uses each month
The number of players connected to one server
The delay between an action and the response arriving
The amount of storage a game takes up on a device
q.why: Latency is delay; low latency is essential in cloud gaming because lag spoils fast-paced games.

q.q: Which is the most important technical requirement for good cloud gaming?
o: A large hard drive to store the games
A powerful graphics card in the device
A fast internet connection with low latency
A disc drive to load the game files
q.why: Because the game is streamed, a fast connection with low latency is essential; storage and graphics power matter much less.

q.q: A player's character reacts half a second after the button is pressed in a streamed racing game. What is the most likely cause?
o: Too little storage on the player's device
The game has not been backed up
High latency on the internet connection
The game was bought as a free demo
q.why: Lag spoils fast-paced games; high latency on the connection causes a delay between input and response.

q.q: Why might cloud gaming be a problem for a player with a limited mobile data allowance?
o: Streaming HD video of the game uses a lot of data
Cloud games must be downloaded in full every time
Cloud saves cannot be stored on mobile networks
Cloud gaming only works over a cable connection
q.why: Streaming HD video uses a lot of data, which is a drawback for players on limited allowances.

q.q: What risk do players face if a cloud gaming service closes?
o: Their console will stop working for disc-based games
Their saved games are automatically moved to a disc
They may lose access to the games they were playing
The latency of their internet connection will rise
q.why: If a service closes or a game is removed, players may lose access to it.

q.q: How do cloud saves benefit a player who uses a console and a phone?
o: Saves are copied onto a disc that works in both devices
Saves are kept in the cloud and synchronised across devices
Saves are deleted after each session to free up storage
Saves can only be loaded on the device that made them
q.why: Saves are kept in the cloud and synchronised, so progress carries across devices.

q.q: Compared with playing from a disc on a console, what is the main dependency of cloud gaming?
o: The power and storage of the device
A disc drive in good working order
A large amount of local storage
A fast, low-latency internet connection
q.why: Disc or console gaming depends on device power and storage; cloud gaming depends on a fast, low-latency connection.

q.q: Which is an impact of the cloud on game PRODUCERS rather than on players?
o: Saves kept in the cloud
High-end games on cheap devices
Less piracy, protecting sales
No need for long downloads
q.why: Less piracy protects producers' sales. The other three are impacts on players.

q.q: Which is a drawback of cloud gaming for players?
o: Games are released instantly
Little local storage is needed
Cheap devices can be used
Subscriptions are ongoing
q.why: Ongoing subscriptions are a drawback; the other three are benefits.

q.q: A quality of written communication question asks about the impact of cloud technology on gaming. Which plan would best meet the mark scheme?
o: Cover producers and players, include benefits and drawbacks, and use terms such as latency
List as many benefits for players as possible in short bullet points
Describe only the benefits for producers, in as much detail as possible
Explain how to set up a cloud gaming account step by step
q.why: QWC answers should be full paragraphs covering producers and players, benefits and drawbacks, using terms like latency, streaming and piracy correctly.

q.q: Why does less piracy matter to the games industry?
o: It lowers the latency for players across the world
It means games no longer need to be updated
It lets producers sell their games on discs again
It protects sales and the money that funds new games
q.why: Less piracy protects sales and the money that funds new games.

q.q: A pupil's laptop crashes while she is writing in a cloud document, but she loses almost nothing. Which feature helped?
o: Version history
Sharing permissions
Pay as you go
Autosave every few seconds
q.why: Many cloud apps save automatically every few seconds, so very little work is lost if a device crashes.

q.q: What does synchronisation mean in cloud storage?
o: The latest version of a file appears on every device
Old versions of a file are deleted to save space
Files are compressed before they are uploaded
Files are scrambled so they cannot be read
q.why: Synchronisation means the latest version appears on your phone, laptop and school PC.

q.q: A teacher edits a worksheet on her laptop at home and next morning the changed version is already on her classroom PC. Which feature is this?
o: Synchronisation
Version history
Autosave
Encryption
q.why: Synchronisation keeps copies up to date so a change appears on every device.

q.q: Which feature lets a team restore an earlier draft of a shared document?
o: Synchronisation
Version history
Autosave
Push alerts
q.why: Version history records who changed what and when, and lets an earlier version be restored.

q.q: Why is sharing a cloud link often better than emailing a large attachment?
o: A link makes the file smaller so that it can be emailed more quickly
Everyone works on one up-to-date copy, with permissions controlling access
Shared links can be opened without any internet connection at all
Attachments cannot contain images, tables or other large content
q.why: Uploading once and sharing a link avoids large attachments and multiple versions, and permissions control who can view, comment or edit.

q.q: When sharing a cloud file, what can permissions control?
o: How quickly the file uploads to the server
How many times the file is backed up each day
Whether each person can view, comment on or edit it
Which device the file was first created on
q.why: Permissions control who can view, comment on or edit each file or folder, and access can be removed later.

q.q: A pupil leaves a group project. What can the owner of the shared folder do?
o: Delete the pupil's account from the provider
Restore the folder to a version before the pupil joined
Change the pupil's password for them
Remove that pupil's access to the folder
q.why: Sharing permissions can be removed later, so the pupil no longer has access.

q.q: What is a collaborative tool?
o: Software that lets several people edit the same document at the same time
Software that copies files onto every device the user owns
Software that blocks unauthorised people from a network
Software that scans uploaded files for known malware
q.why: Collaborative tools such as Google Docs, Microsoft 365 online and Teams let several people edit the same document at once.

q.q: Which of these is an example of a collaborative tool?
o: A USB memory stick
Microsoft Teams
A local file server
An external hard drive
q.why: Teams, Google Docs, Sheets and Slides and Microsoft 365 online are collaborative tools.

q.q: A group of four pupils edits a shared presentation at the same time. What do they see?
o: A separate copy each, merged together at the end
Each other's changes appearing almost instantly
Only their own changes until they log out
A locked file until the first pupil has finished
q.why: In collaborative tools each person sees others' changes appear almost instantly.

q.q: What does version history record?
o: Which devices the file was opened on
Who changed what and when
How much storage the file uses
Which users are allowed to edit
q.why: Version history records who changed what and when, and allows an earlier version to be restored.

q.q: A teammate accidentally deletes half of a shared report. What is the best way to recover it?
o: Wait for synchronisation to put the text back
Ask the provider to buy more storage space
Change the sharing permissions to view only
Restore an earlier version using version history
q.why: Version history lets an earlier version be restored if something goes wrong. Synchronisation would simply copy the deletion to every device.

q.q: Which is a risk of collaboration in the cloud?
o: Wrong permissions can expose a file to the wrong people
Files cannot be opened on more than one device
Changes made by others are never saved
Only one person can comment on a document
q.why: Wrong permissions can expose a file, and anyone with edit rights can change or delete content.

q.q: What happens to many cloud files when a user deletes them?
o: They are kept in a recycle bin for a time
They are immediately and permanently erased
They are copied to every shared user's device
They are moved onto the user's local drive
q.why: Many services keep deleted files in a recycle bin for a time.

q.q: How do cloud providers protect files if one of their servers fails?
o: They keep copies on several servers and can restore files
They email every file back to the user each night
They ask users to keep a USB copy of all their work
They move the files onto the user's own laptop
q.why: Providers keep copies on several servers and can restore files; users need no technical knowledge.

q.q: Which measures should users take to keep their cloud storage account secure?
o: A strong password and two-factor authentication
Sharing their password only with close friends
Turning off synchronisation on all devices
Saving all files as read-only documents
q.why: Users must keep their account secure with a strong password and two-factor authentication.

q.q: Which answer best explains a benefit of collaborative tools for a team, as examiners want?
o: Version history is one of the features found in collaborative tools
Collaborative tools are very useful and good for teams to use
Teams can collaborate using collaborative tools online
Version history lets the team restore an earlier draft if mistakes are made
q.why: Name the feature and explain the benefit. Only the first answer does both.

q.q: How can collaborative tools keep a team up to date when a shared file changes?
o: They delete the old file and send a new attachment
They lock the file until everyone has read it
They print a copy for each member of the team
They can send an email alert when a file changes
q.why: Users can be alerted by email when a file changes.

q.q: In a group project, a pupil wants to suggest a change to a classmate's paragraph without editing it. Which feature should she use?
o: Version history
Comments
Synchronisation
Autosave
q.why: Collaborative tools let users leave comments, so suggestions can be made without changing the text.

q.q: Why is synchronisation not a substitute for version history?
o: Synchronisation only works on files that are stored on a USB stick
Synchronisation deletes all files that are older than one week
A mistake is copied to every device, so an earlier version is still needed
Synchronisation can only be used by one person at a time
q.why: Synchronisation copies the latest version, including any mistake, everywhere; version history is what lets an earlier version be restored.
